We quantified the concentrations of 222 Rn, 220 Rn, CH 4 and CO 2 during experiments at an air flow rate of ~0.2 L min -1 once every hour while operating the diffusion pump in the SARAD ® RTM 2200. This small flow rate is inadequate for accurate measurements of 220 Rn owing to its short half-life of only 55.6 sec [ Hursh , 1966] and partial decay under conditions of slow flow into the measurement chamber. 220 Rn radiation intensity was either measured via α-spectroscopy at a faster flow rate of 1 L min -1 in 10-min increments (n ≥ 10) while temporarily operating the more powerful membrane pump, or values from flow rates of ≤ 0.2 L min -1 with the diffusion pump were doubled to adjust for fast 220 Rn decay (see supporting information of Schimmelmann et al. [in review] for detailed control experiments and graphed data). α-Spectroscopic measurements of 222 Rn abundance were not affected by flow rate and were based on a ‘slow measurement’ algorithm that uses 218 Po and 214 Po daughter decay as proxies for 222 Rn [ SARAD ® GmbH , 2017]. Ultrapure nitrogen gas and Scotty gas mixtures (Sigma-Aldrich) were used for calibration of gas concentrations with precisions of ± 1 ppmv for CH 4 and ± 100 ppmv for CO 2 (± 95 % confidence intervals). References: Hursh JB. Thoron half-life. J. Inorg. Nucl. Chem. 1966; 28 (12): 2771-2776. https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1902(66)80001-5 SARAD ® GmbH. Available from: https://www.sarad.de/cms/media/docs/applikation/AN_007_RadonBasics_PPT_EN_11-04-08.pdf Schimmelmann A, Fernandez Cortes A, Cuezva S, Streil T, Lennon JT. Radiolysis via radioactivity is not responsible for rapid methane oxidation in subterranean air. PLOS ONE , in review.

We conducted a number of experiments to test for the effects of radiation and microbial activity on CH 4 dynamics in our experimental apparatus. Multi-day time-series of data were collected in closed-circuit air reflux mode (i) as duplicated blank experiments without added radon or thoron, (ii) with enhanced 220 Rn concentration in dry or moist air, (iii) with enhanced 222 Rn concentration in dry or moist air, and (iv) with jointly enhanced 220 Rn and 222 Rn concentrations in moist air to depict an extreme scenario where cave air had a highly elevated α-radiation level. Furthermore, (v) we tested for CH 4 oxidation after placing moist soil, which we assumed contained methanotrophic bacteria (MOB), into the 5-L glass flask, without elevated radioactivity. Certain impurities in industrially conditioned natural gas may act as MOB inhibitors, for example acetylene and carbon monoxide [ Oremland and Capone , 1988, p. 335]. As a precaution, the CH 4 spikes in experiments employing soils were derived from gas that was collected from a natural seepage of shale gas in New York State. The flammable shale gas contained CH 4 , ethane and propane in volume ratios of 77.8 : 15.3 : 6.9 [ Farhan Ul Haque et al ., 2018]. Natural shale gas is not known to contain acetylene or carbon monoxide. Soil #1 from the bank of Pipe Creek was collected fresh near a seepage of natural gas in New York State on June 16, 2017 (Erie County, Town of Colden, 42° 41.6 N, 78° 41.2 W), kept cool during transport, and was deployed in the apparatus on June 18, 2017. Soil #2 was collected on July 11, 2017 from a grassy area behind the building of the Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, in Bloomington, Indiana (39° 10.35 N, 86° 31.31 W), kept moist at room temperature, and was deployed in the apparatus on July 12, 2017. steps.title: Assemble IU recirculating apparatus
steps.instruction: Construct a sealed recirculating system using a 5 L round‑bottom borosilicate flask with three standard 24/40 tapered ground‑glass ports (one closed with a glass stopper). Connect 9 mm o.d. Pyrex® glass tubes and short segments of Tygon® tubing to a SARAD® RTM‑2200 gas‑analytical instrument equipped with internal pumps and an Axetris® laser methane detector. Minimize the use of gas‑permeable plastic tubing and install optional pinch clamps to isolate the uranium‑ore tube if desired. The total sealed volume of the circuit should be approximately 6 L.

steps.title: Prepare radon sources
steps.instruction: Place 6.4 g of a dry, porous co‑precipitate of thorium carbonate and nickel carbonate (weight ratio 100 : 22) into the receiving port of the 5 L flask to generate 220 Rn (thoron). For 222 Rn, load a 9 cm layer of uranium‑ore chips into a vertically mounted 35 mm i.d. glass tube that runs parallel to a 9 mm o.d. glass tube; add a 25 mm layer of 6‑14 mesh coconut charcoal (Fisher Scientific) on top of the ore as a filter to adsorb co‑produced 220 Rn. Use pinch clamps to isolate or force flow through the uranium‑ore tube as required.

steps.title: Spike air mixture
steps.instruction: Introduce air into the sealed ~6 L circuit and spike it to approximately 70 ppmv methane (CH₄) using natural‑gas methane and to about 5 000 ppmv carbon dioxide (CO₂) (omit CO₂ spike for experiments that include soil). Optionally add moist soil, a wet tissue, or deionized water to the bottom of the flask to modify humidity.

steps.title: Adjust relative humidity
steps.instruction: Set the experiment to either low humidity (~50–56 % RH) by using relatively dry laboratory air, or high humidity (~100 % RH) by suspending a wet paper towel inside the flask. Alternatively, raise humidity by adding moist soil and/or deionized water to the flask bottom. Note that higher humidity enhances radon emanation from the solid sources.

steps.title: Start recirculation and log data
steps.instruction: Activate the SARAD® RTM‑2200 internal pumps to recirculate the air continuously. The instrument logs temperature, pressure, flow, battery voltage, and relative humidity on an hourly basis. Because the SARAD internal pump and electronics raise the recorded temperature by ~10 °C above room temperature, subtract this offset to obtain room‑temperature‑corrected values and compute adjusted relative humidity.

steps.title: Validate SARAD measurements (optional)
steps.instruction: Place ~5 L of air containing the same radon sources into a sealed plastic bag. Recirculate the bag air through the SARAD® RTM‑2200 at 1 L min⁻¹ while a newly calibrated Thoron Scout instrument records temperature, humidity, pressure, and 220 Rn/222 Rn concentrations in 10‑min intervals. Allow a 2 h warm‑up period; keep the air turbulent with a small fan. Compare the two data sets to confirm compatibility.

steps.title: Set up RHUL terrarium experiment
steps.instruction: Use a gas‑tight glass terrarium (wall thickness 5 mm; width 3.45 cm; length 1.92 cm; height 20.3 cm; volume 13.45 L) with a hermetically greased 40.6 × 24.0 cm glass cover. Seal three 6‑mm o.d. ports with O‑rings and vacuum grease. Connect the first port to an external micro‑diaphragm pump that draws 99.9 % pure N₂ from a 3‑L Tedlar® bag at 3.1 L min⁻¹. Route the N₂ through a T‑connector into two 3‑L Tedlar® bags inside the terrarium; displaced air exits via the second port into an empty 1‑L Tedlar® bag for sampling. Place two 5‑cm‑diameter uraninite‑bearing pitchblende fragments inside the terrarium. Install an AlphaLab Air Ion Counter (30‑s intervals, 0–2 × 10⁷ ions m⁻³) with an integrated fan, and a Canary Pro α‑monitor (1‑h intervals, uncertainty < 8 % above 350 Bq m⁻³) in a passive diffusion chamber.

steps.title: Run RHUL experiment #1 (stage 1)
steps.instruction: Flush the terrarium with laboratory air (no pitchblende, no water) and monitor ion concentration and 222 Rn for ~6 h (stage 1).

steps.title: Run RHUL experiment #1 (stage 2)
steps.instruction: Add the two pitchblende fragments and a beaker containing 130 mL of water pre‑heated to 38 °C. Continue monitoring for an additional ~15 h (stage 2) to achieve elevated relative humidity (>85 %) and increased 222 Rn levels.

steps.title: Run RHUL experiment #2
steps.instruction: In the same terrarium, place pitchblende fragments and the 130 mL 38 °C water from the start. Run the experiment for 76 h 50 min; after ~5 h the 222 Rn‑based radiation level should exceed 50 kBq m⁻³. Collect ~1‑L air aliquots in Tedlar® bags on four occasions for later analysis.

steps.title: Analyze CH₄ samples
steps.instruction: Analyze each ~1‑L Tedlar® bag sample with a Picarro G1301 CRDS (Cavity Ring‑Down Spectrometer) at the Greenhouse Gas Research Group (RHUL). Calibrate the spectrometer against NOAA reference gases. Run each analysis for 3 min; the measurement uncertainty is ±0.5 ppb CH₄.
